The White-rumped tanager Cypsnagra hirundinacea, a distinctive passerine of the South American cerrado, exhibits life-history traits tightly linked to its thermally variable environment. Eggs incubated at a stable temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] produce hatchlings after a development period of 16 days [ab = 16 days]. At emergence, the wet weight at birth is a modest 2.7 grams [Wwb = 2.7 grams], a value that places this species among the smaller-bodied thraupids. This initial mass is eclipsed by the gains achieved over the nestling period, as the developing chick progresses toward its adult dimensions. Under the elevated body temperatures typical of active adult foraging, which can exceed 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the species demonstrates a rapid developmental schedule in its early post-hatching phase. Field records indicate that fledging occurs at 12.1 days after hatching [tx = 12.1 days after hatching], a short nestling duration consistent with an altricial strategy that prioritizes early departure from the nest, presumably to mitigate predation risks in the open grasslands it inhabits at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

Sexual maturation in this species follows a relatively protracted trajectory when compared to other Neotropical tanagers of similar body mass. The onset of puberty is estimated at 36.3 days after hatching [tp = 36.3 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at an active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This value, derived from captive-rearing studies, suggests that gonadal development requires a substantial thermal input to complete, a pattern also observed in congeners occupying similar xeric habitats. Following puberty, there is a further delay before the initiation of breeding activity. The time since birth at first brood, representing the interval from hatching to the production of the first clutch, is approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days] under analogous thermal conditions. This year-long wait before first reproduction is noteworthy, as it implies that first-year birds defer breeding until their second calendar year, a life-history tactic that may allow juveniles to accumulate sufficient body reserves and to secure a breeding territory in a landscape where suitable nesting sites are limited and competition is intense.

Body mass trajectories across the life cycle of Cypsnagra hirundinacea reveal a substantial increase from the neonatal stage to adulthood. The initial wet weight of newly hatched nestlings is approximately 3.0 grams [Ww0 = approximately 3.0 grams], representing the mass of the chick immediately after hatching and before the onset of parental feeding. This value is nearly identical to the recorded wet weight at birth of 2.7 grams [Wwb = 2.7 grams], indicating minimal mass loss during the transition from the egg to the external environment. From this modest starting point, the nestlings undergo a period of rapid somatic growth fueled by intensive biparental provisioning. Observations of free-living birds indicate that the ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults, measured as the asymptotic mass, reaches 31.3 grams [Wwi = 31.3 grams]. This final adult mass reflects a roughly tenfold increase over the neonatal weight, a growth multiple that is typical for altricial passerines and that underscores the efficiency with which these birds convert insect prey into new tissue during the brief nestling and fledgling phases.

The demographic lifespan of the White-rumped tanager is comparatively long for a passerine of its body size, a pattern that aligns with its delayed reproduction and relatively low annual fecundity. Mark-recapture studies conducted in the Brazilian Cerrado have documented that the maximum recorded longevity, or lifespan, is approximately 4.8 years [am = approximately 4.8 years] when birds are active at a typical body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This extended survival window, which corresponds to roughly 1752 days, is unusual among thraupids of comparable mass. It suggests that adult mortality rates are low, likely due to the species' effective predator avoidance behaviors and its relatively stable cerrado environment, which lacks the extreme seasonal bottlenecks that drive high adult turnover in more arid-adapted tanagers. The coupling of a long lifespan with a late age at first breeding points toward a slow life-history pace, in which individuals invest heavily in self-maintenance and survival early in life before committing to reproduction.

Reproductive output in the White-rumped tanager is modest and carefully timed to align with the peak abundance of arthropod prey in the cerrado during the rainy season. Females typically produce a clutch of 4 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 4 eggs per nesting attempt], a fixed clutch size that shows little variation across the species' geographic range. The frequency with which these clutches are produced is limited by the length of the breeding season and the energetic demands of incubation and chick-rearing. Available field data indicate that pairs typically attempt 1 breeding event per year [F_R_i = 1 breeding event per year], yielding an annual reproductive output of 4 eggs per year. This low frequency of reproduction, measured here under the species' active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], stands in contrast to the multi-brooded strategies of many temperate-zone passerines. The combination of a small clutch and a single annual brood, coupled with a long lifespan and delayed first reproduction, firmly places Cypsnagra hirundinacea on the slow end of the passerine life-history continuum, a strategy likely shaped by the predictability and seasonality of its cerrado habitat.
